Issued at 217 PM CDT Sat Sep 12 2026

Elongated area of high pressure stretching from the Dakotas and 
northwestward into Canada will bring overall dry weather for the 
rest of the afternoon continuing through late this evening. However, 
above the surface high a belt of stronger zonal to slight northwest 
winds aloft (60-80kts, highest ND/SD/MN border) on the southwestern 
side of the large upper level low over east-central Canada (and 
within a northwest to southeast oriented shortwave circling around 
it over ND/MN) could be enough to generate some spotty to bands of 
elevated rain showers overnight through Sunday morning. Several of 
the CAMs do show these potential bands highlighting portions of 
north central/northeastern SD/ND border and an area over south 
central to east central SD. Latest NBM pops really only had pops 
over south central so blended in ECAM to the mix to increase 
coverage and pops for these areas, especially with what HRRR/REFS is 
indicating. The caveat to this is the drier air at the lower levels 
from this high as EC/RAP soundings show this. Due to this, QPF is 
expected to be light with any rain potential up to a couple 
hundredths at most. Not much in the way of MUCAPE overnight but bulk 
shear will be around 50kts, however, mid level lapse rates are weak. 
No severe weather is anticipated but cannot not rule out weak 
thunderstorms over south central/east central SD as HREF Z>40dbz 
does highlight this potential where more convective cells are 
possible. Any heavier rain shower/storm will lead to higher QPF. 

An upper level trough originating from the PacNW will track east and 
northeast across the Northern Rockies through the Northern Plains 
and into Canada Monday morning through Tuesday morning along with 
its surface low/cold front. This wave and its low is forecast to 
deepen to around 998mb over ND/Canada border Monday 
afternoon/evening. GEFS is a bit further north and a few millibars 
deeper (996mb) than the EC at this time therefore a bit lower 
confidence in exact track and intensity for now. With the region 
within the PVA of the UL wave in southwest flow and east of the sfc 
low with low level winds out of the south/southeast, this provides 
lift aloft and also ushers in moisture as dewpoints will increase 
into the 60s and PWAT values will increase to around 1.2 to 1.6" 
ahead of the cold front within the warm sector. Highest PWAT values 
are around the 99th percentile for this time of year and 2-3 
standard deviations above climo per NAEFS. With this setup and 
moisture, models seem to be pretty consistent leading to higher 
confidence on widespread rain moving in over central SD late early 
Monday morning (pops 80%+) with the rain spreading east and 
northeast and over the entire CWA by Monday morning through the 
afternoon (80-100% pops along and east of Mo River). As the 
low/front tracks east/northeast, rain will diminish west to east 
across the CWA Monday afternoon over central SD with the last of the 
rain exiting the eastern CWA Monday evening. Wind shear of 40kts 
will be present, however, the better instability looks to remain 
south and southeast of the region, therefore, no severe weather is 
anticipated for now with just the potential for weak thunderstorms 
given this shear and higher winds aloft and marginal instability. 
Looking at the 06Z run of the ensembles, ENS mean QPF ranges from 
0.3-0.7" (highest over eastern/southeastern SD) while GEFS is drier 
given the more northern track with values of around 0.2-0.4" for the 
24 hours ending at 06Z Tuesday. NBM probability of rainfall half 
inch or more is 60-80% and one inch or more 40-50%, with the inch 
prob mainly over northeastern SD/MN. High end scenario (wetter/more 
southern track of low), rainfall would be between 1-2" and low end 
scenario (northern track/drier) would be under a half inch.

With the passage of the cold front and steepening of the low level 
lapse rates, winds will increase Monday over central SD early and 
spread eastward with the front with gusts of 30-40kts by late 
morning/afternoon. The cooler airmass overhead will continue through 
the rest of the weekend with temps about 5-10 degrees below normal 
for this time of year and highs overall in the 60s Sunday. Warmer 
air per return flow on Monday will lead to warmer temps mainly west 
of the James River with highs across the CWA in the upper 60s to 
upper 70s.
